title: From Passenger to Driver in Your Career
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: This is the third part of Chiarelli's series on leadership and careers, and it argues that careers accelerate through a handful of deliberate choices rather than titles or performance ratings. She offers three sentences she wishes she had been told earlier: stop waiting for permission, choose carefully who you work with, and accept that not failing at anything means not growing. Each principle is anchored in a short personal anecdote, such as proposing a process improvement unasked, drifting into a cynical project team, and running a workshop that partly flopped. The move she makes is to recast a career from something that happens to you into something you design, with agency, environment and discomfort as levers you can pull. She is careful to say this is not a call to chase chaos, since recklessness is not growth. The piece closes with three reflection questions for the reader, which makes it usable as a self-coaching prompt for emerging leaders.
points: Opportunities that change your trajectory usually go to people who act as if they already have partial permission and bring a concrete proposal rather than waiting for an invitation.
Your colleagues set your sense of normal, including how rigorous your thinking is, how you handle setbacks and what you believe is possible, so choosing projects and rooms is a career decision.
Comfort is an unreliable guide because it can signal thriving or simply that you have stopped stretching; small, survivable failures are evidence you are working at the edge of your skill.
Her workshop failure shows a practical recovery habit, writing down what worked and what to redesign from scratch, which turned a flat session into a far stronger one.
quotes: I used to treat development as something that other people organised for me. I waited for training budgets and formal programmes.

Over time, two things happened. First, I realised that people rarely come and tap you on the shoulder when opportunities are available. Second, I noticed that other people around me were moving faster because they volunteered for messy work and suggested ideas rather than waiting to be briefed.

The lesson here is that the opportunities that change your trajectory often start with you acting as if you already have partial permission. You can test the waters with a concrete proposal instead of waiting for a perfectly timed invitation (which, by the way, may never come!).

We like to think of our careers as individual journeys: our skills and our effort. But time has shown me just how much we are shaped by the people around us: by their standards, habits, fears and ambitions.

Obviously, you can’t always choose your manager or your immediate team. But you often have more choice than you think: which projects you volunteer for, whose feedback you seek out, which rooms you spend time in and how long you stay once you’ve understood the culture. Changing jobs is hard, but it’s often on the table.
Failure in this context wasn’t a dramatic collapse or a career-ending mistake. It was simply evidence that I was operating at the edge of my current skillset.
Growth usually feels awkward up close, and you only recognise it as progress when you look back and see that what you can now do once felt impossible.
